T1: Consumers will adopt differentiated consumer gloves if they perceive them as a lifestyle or fashion accessory, leading to multiple purchases and premium pricing. How value is captured: Ansell can sell through its own retail channels or third-party consumer brands at higher margins than industrial sales.. Assumptions: Consumers currently view industrial gloves as functional only.; Fashion awareness among target consumers is sufficient to shift purchase behavior.; Ansell can design and market gloves with aesthetic appeal without compromising protection.. Predictions: In a test offering a differentiated consumer glove at a premium price, purchase intent will be higher than for a standard industrial glove.; Surveyed consumers will cite style as a primary reason for purchase.; Repeat purchase rate will be higher for the differentiated glove compared to a generic industrial glove..

Test "Consumer Glove Preference Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.. Sample: 500 adult consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region (Australia, UK, US, Europe).. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: "Would buy this differentiated glove?"), WTP (€), and primary purchase reason (open-ended).. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent and WTP for the differentiated glove when it is positioned as a lifestyle/fashion accessory compared to a standard industrial glove.; T2: Higher purchase intent and WTP for the differentiated glove when it is positioned as a medical necessity for a specific health condition compared to a standard industrial glove.. Decision rule: If purchase intent for the differentiated glove (lifestyle) is at least 15 percentage points higher than for the differentiated glove (medical necessity) AND the WTP for the lifestyle version is at least €20 higher than the medical version, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition for lifestyle use. If not, continue focusing on industrial segment.. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting lifestyle/fashion use cases, starting with a limited pilot to test purchase intent and willingness-to-pay. If the pilot shows sufficient demand, scale the proposition through direct-to-consumer channels and third-party consumer brands. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns warehouse packing efficiency and does not address consumer perception of gloves as lifestyle or fashion items. Therefore it does not affect T1. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-D.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting lifestyle/fashion use cases, starting with a limited pilot to test purchase intent and willingness-to-pay. If the pilot shows sufficient demand, scale the proposition through direct-to-consumer channels and third-party consumer brands. Target customer: Individual consumers who view protective gloves as a lifestyle accessory, particularly those in age groups and geographic regions where fashion and personal style are important (e.g., young adults, urban consumers).. Value proposition: A differentiated glove that combines protection with aesthetic design, positioned as a fashion item rather than a purely functional industrial product, allowing premium pricing and multiple purchases.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Consumer Glove Preference Test (500 respondents, 10 weeks, €15,000) to compare purchase intent and willingness-to-pay for a lifestyle versus medical positioning.. Uncertainty: The size of the consumer market for differentiated gloves and the willingness to pay a premium are unknown. The test will resolve whether demand exists and whether it can be captured profitably.. Would change if: If the test shows purchase intent for the lifestyle version is at least 15 percentage points lower than for the medical version, or if willingness-to-pay for the lifestyle version is at least €20 lower, we would abandon the lifestyle focus.; If new evidence shows strong consumer demand for medical gloves (e.g., sales data for specialized gloves or explicit consumer statements about health necessity), we would shift focus to T2.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Participants indicate whether they would purchase each kit and cite reasons (privacy/convenience vs cost/need).. Sample: 400 adult respondents recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region to reflect U.S. households. Randomly assigned to see either the premium-priced kit or the low-cost kit.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: would purchase) and primary reason (open-ended) for choosing each kit.. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent for the premium-priced kit and higher frequency of citing privacy/convenience as the primary reason.; T2: Higher purchase intent for the low-cost kit and higher frequency of citing cost/need as the primary reason.. Decision rule: If the premium-priced kit achieves purchase intent ≥ 40% and privacy/convenience reasons ≥ 30% of respondents, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition for home CPR training. If the low-cost kit achieves purchase intent ≥ 40% and cost/need reasons ≥ 30%, consider a low‑cost consumer offering. If neither meets threshold, recommend no expansion.. Cost: 15000 euros, 8 weeks.

Measure: Purchase intent measured as a binary choice: “Would you buy this device at the price?” (yes/no). Predictions: T1: Brand trust variant will achieve at least 15% higher purchase intent than health concern variant.; T2: Health concern variant will achieve at least 15% higher purchase intent than brand trust variant.. Decision rule: If the difference in purchase intent between the two variants is >=15 percentage points, the corresponding theory is supported. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: "Would you buy this product?") and willingness to pay (WTP) on a 7‑point scale. Secondary measure: stated trust in Dräger as a medical brand (1–10).. Decision rule: If purchase intent for Group A exceeds Group B by at least 10 percentage points, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (supporting T1). T1: Consumers will adopt home CPR training if they perceive it as a medical necessity and a way to protect family members, leading to higher purchase intent and willingness to pay. Who benefits: Individual consumers (families) who need to learn CPR for emergency situations.. Why behaviour changes: If consumers view home CPR training as a critical life-saving skill, they will be motivated to acquire it, especially if it is presented as a medical necessity and can be shared with family members.. How value is captured: Laerdal can capture value through premium pricing, subscription models for updates, and direct-to-consumer sales of kits, leveraging its existing CPR technology and brand reputation.. Assumptions: Consumers trust medical recommendations and are willing to invest in home training.; Home CPR training is perceived as a medical necessity rather than a lifestyle product.; Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a product that can be shared within families.. Predictions: Surveyed consumers will express higher purchase intent when framed as a medical necessity versus a lifestyle item.; Willingness to pay for home CPR kits will be higher when presented as a family protection tool versus a general fitness product.; Sales data will show higher conversion rates for home kits marketed as medical necessity versus general fitness..

T2: Consumers will adopt home CPR training if they perceive it as a convenient, low-cost way to learn a life-saving skill, leading to higher purchase intent and willingness to pay. Who benefits: Individual consumers (families) who need to learn CPR for emergency situations and value convenience and affordability.. Why behaviour changes: If consumers view home CPR training as a quick, affordable way to acquire a critical skill, they will be motivated to acquire it, especially if it can be done at home without specialized training.. How value is captured: Laerdal can capture value through lower-margin direct-to-consumer sales of kits, subscription models for updates, and potential licensing of the core CPR technology to consumer electronics brands.. Assumptions: Consumers prioritize convenience and cost over professional training.; Home CPR training is perceived as accessible and easy to learn.; Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a product that can be used at home without specialized equipment.. Predictions: Surveyed consumers will express higher purchase intent when framed as convenient and affordable versus a medical necessity.; Willingness to pay for home CPR kits will be higher when presented as a low-cost, at-home solution versus a premium medical necessity.; Sales data will show higher conversion rates for home kits marketed as convenient versus a medical necessity..

Test "Consumer Messaging Test: Medical Necessity vs Convenience" between T1; T2. Method: Online controlled experiment with two landing pages for the same home CPR kit, each presented to a separate segment of potential consumers. Participants view the landing page for 10 seconds and are asked to indicate whether they would purchase the kit if framed as a medical necessity (T1) or as a convenient, low-cost way to learn CPR (T2). They are then asked about willingness to pay (if they would pay a premium).. Sample: 500 adult consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced across two segments (250 per segment) to ensure random assignment. Recruitment target: individuals who have expressed interest in learning CPR for family emergencies or general health awareness.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy) and willingness to pay (if they would pay a premium). Secondary: self-reported perceived importance of medical necessity versus convenience.. Predictions: T1: Segment exposed to medical necessity framing will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than the convenience framing segment.; T2: Segment exposed to convenience framing will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than the medical necessity framing segment.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent for the medical necessity framing segment exceeds that of the convenience framing segment by at least 10 percentage points across both segments, we conclude T1 is more likely. If the difference is less than 10 percentage points, we conclude neither framing significantly drives purchase intent, and we recommend further testing.. Cost: 15000 euros, 8 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for home CPR training that emphasizes medical necessity and family protection, using premium pricing and direct-to-consumer sales. Begin with a limited launch of a home kit marketed as a critical life-saving skill, and gather consumer feedback before scaling. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns warehouse packing efficiency and does not address consumer demand, willingness to pay, or home CPR training. Therefore it does not affect T1. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-D.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for home CPR training that emphasizes medical necessity and family protection, using premium pricing and direct-to-consumer sales. Begin with a limited launch of a home kit marketed as a critical life-saving skill, and gather consumer feedback before scaling. Target customer: Individual consumers (families) who need to learn CPR for emergency situations and are willing to invest in a product framed as a medical necessity.. Value proposition: A home CPR kit that positions learning as a critical life-saving skill, leveraging Laerdal’s existing CPR technology and brand reputation to justify premium pricing and capture value through direct sales and potential subscription models.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Consumer Messaging Test (8 weeks, €15,000) to compare purchase intent and willingness to pay under medical necessity versus convenience framing. Use results to decide whether to proceed with a full consumer launch.. Uncertainty: The actual willingness to pay for a premium-priced home CPR kit is unknown; consumer demand for home training is uncertain; the competitive landscape for consumer CPR products is unclear.. Would change if: If the test shows purchase intent for the convenience framing segment significantly exceeds that for the medical necessity framing segment by at least 10 percentage points, we would reconsider the premium-pricing strategy and explore a more; affordable, subscription-based model.; If new evidence shows strong consumer demand for home CPR training and high willingness to pay, we would reconsider the investment.; If Laerdal secures a partnership with a consumer brand or electronics company to co‑brand or distribute the kit, we would reassess the direct‑to‑consumer approach.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1: Homeowners will purchase Kingspan insulation if they perceive it as a safety-critical product for fire resistance, because they will choose products marketed as compliant with building codes and safety standards. Who benefits: Kingspan gains premium pricing and brand association with safety, while homeowners gain confidence in product performance.. Why behaviour changes: Safety concerns drive homeowners to select insulation that meets regulatory requirements, even if it is more expensive, because they want to avoid fire hazards and ensure compliance.. How value is captured: Kingspan can charge a premium price for safety-certified insulation and capture value through higher margins and brand loyalty.. Assumptions: Homeowners are aware of Grenfell Tower fire and associated safety concerns.; They prioritize fire resistance over cost in insulation purchases.; Kingspan can effectively communicate safety compliance in consumer messaging.. Predictions: In a survey, homeowners will indicate willingness to pay at least 15% more for fire‑resistant insulation.; Purchase intent will be higher for Kingspan products labeled as "fire‑resistant" compared to unmarked products.; Sales of safety‑certified insulation will increase in regions with strict building codes..

T2: Homeowners will purchase Kingspan insulation if they perceive it as a cost‑effective, energy‑efficiency solution that reduces long‑term heating costs, because they seek to lower utility bills and improve home value. Who benefits: Kingspan gains volume sales and market penetration, while homeowners gain lower ongoing expenses and potential home‑value appreciation.. Why behaviour changes: Energy‑cost sensitivity and desire for lower utility bills motivate homeowners to choose insulation that promises reduced heating requirements, even if upfront cost is higher.. How value is captured: Kingspan can sell larger volumes at higher unit margins and capture value through recurring sales of insulation and potential partnerships with energy‑efficiency programs.. Assumptions: Homeowners are aware of energy‑efficiency benefits of insulation.; They are willing to invest in insulation that pays for itself over time.; Kingspan can communicate energy‑savings claims effectively to consumers.. Test "Homeowner Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants view a product description of Kingspan insulation and are asked to indicate willingness to pay a premium (15% for safety, 10% for energy efficiency) and to choose which message they would click on.. Sample: 500 UK homeowners recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, income, and home ownership.. Measure: Percentage of participants who indicate willingness to pay the specified premium and choose the corresponding message.. Predictions: T1: At least 35% will choose the safety message and indicate willingness to pay the 15% premium.; T2: At least 35% will choose the energy efficiency message and indicate willingness to pay the 10% premium.. Decision rule: If the safety message receives ≥35% of choices and ≥35% of participants indicate willingness to pay the 15% premium, proceed to develop a differentiated safety‑focused consumer proposition. If the energy efficiency message receives ≥35% of choices and ≥35% indicate willingness to pay the 10% premium, develop an energy‑efficiency proposition. If neither meets the thresholds, abandon expansion.. Cost: 18000 euros, 8 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes fire safety compliance and compliance with building codes, rather than energy efficiency. Use the existing direct-to-consumer sales channel to reach homeowners and communicate safety credentials. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes fire safety compliance and building code certification, leveraging Kingspan’s existing direct-to-consumer sales channel to reach homeowners. Use the safety message to communicate compliance and safety credentials, and price accordingly to capture premium margins. Target customer: Homeowners in the UK and Europe who are planning or have recently undertaken home improvements, particularly those in regions with strict building codes and safety concerns.. Value proposition: A safety‑certified insulation product that meets or exceeds fire resistance standards, marketed as a reliable, code‑compliant solution that provides peace of mind and compliance, justifying a premium price.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Homeowner Messaging Test (or a smaller pilot) to validate willingness to pay a 15% premium for safety messaging. If the test meets the thresholds, develop a safety‑focused consumer proposition; otherwise, consider other B2B. Uncertainty: The size of the consumer market and the exact willingness to pay for safety‑certified insulation are uncertain. Evidence shows Kingspan already sells directly to end‑users, but it does not reveal consumer demand or price sensitivity.. Would change if: If the test shows the energy‑efficiency message receives at least 35% of choices and willingness to pay the 10% premium, we would shift focus to an energy‑efficiency proposition.; If new evidence demonstrates strong consumer demand for safety‑certified insulation at premium prices, we would reconsider the safety‑focused proposition.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated digital kitchen scale for home food weighing primarily because it provides a more accurate measure of carbohydrate content, which is important for diabetes management. Who benefits: Individual consumers with diabetes who need precise food weight measurements to track carbohydrate intake.. Why behaviour changes: Increased awareness of carbohydrate counting and the need for accurate food weighing drives demand for a digital scale that offers precise measurements.. How value is captured: Mettler-Toledo can capture value by selling a premium-priced digital scale through direct channels, leveraging its brand reputation for precision and its existing sales force.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a digital scale that provides accurate carbohydrate measurements.; Diabetes awareness and carbohydrate counting are growing among home cooks.; Mettler-Toledo can effectively communicate the accuracy advantage to target consumers.. Predictions: In a test offering a digital kitchen scale with carbohydrate measurement features, purchase intent among diabetes patients will be at least 20% higher than for a standard digital scale.; Surveyed consumers will cite carbohydrate accuracy as the primary reason for choosing the product..

T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated digital kitchen scale for home food weighing primarily because it offers convenience and faster weighing compared to manual methods, making it attractive for busy households. Who benefits: Households with limited time for food preparation who need quick, accurate measurements.. Why behaviour changes: Time-saving benefits and the desire for convenience drive demand for a digital scale that reduces weighing time and effort.. How value is captured: Mettler-Toledo can capture value by selling a compact, user-friendly digital scale through direct channels, leveraging its brand for precision and its existing sales force.. Assumptions: Consumers prioritize speed and ease of use over carbohydrate accuracy.; Digital scales are perceived as more convenient than manual scales.; Mettler-Toledo can effectively communicate convenience advantages to target consumers.. Predictions: In a test offering a digital kitchen scale with quick-weighing features, purchase intent among busy households will be at least 20% higher than for a standard digital scale.; Surveyed consumers will cite convenience as the primary reason for choosing the product..

Test "Digital Kitchen Scale Preference Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario and choice between two digital kitchen scales: (1) carbohydrate‑accurate digital scale (features precise weight measurement for carbohydrate counting) and (2) convenience‑focused digital scale (features quick-weighing, compact design, and easy-to-use interface). Participants are randomly assigned to view either scale description or both. They are then asked to indicate their willingness to pay (in euros) and likelihood to purchase (1‑10 scale).. Sample: 500 U.S. adults recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and self-reported interest in diabetes management or busy household routines.. Measure: Average willingness to pay (EUR) and purchase intent (1‑10 scale) for each participant.. Predictions: T1: Participants viewing the carbohydrate‑accurate scale will report higher willingness to pay and purchase intent than those viewing the convenience scale.; T2: Participants viewing the convenience scale will report higher willingness to pay and purchase intent than those viewing the carbohydrate‑accurate scale.. Decision rule: If the average willingness to pay for the carbohydrate‑accurate scale exceeds the average willingness to pay for the convenience scale by at least €5, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition focused on carbohydrate accuracy. If the difference is less than €5, the test is inconclusive and further research is needed.. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes carbohydrate accuracy for individuals with diabetes, using the existing direct sales force to reach this segment. Begin with a limited pilot offering a digital kitchen scale with carbohydrate measurement features, and gather willingness-to-pay data before scaling. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns warehouse packing efficiency and does not address consumer demand for carbohydrate-accurate digital scales. Therefore it does not affect T1. New claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated digital kitchen scale for home food weighing primarily because it provides a more accurate measure of carbohydrate content, which is important for diabetes management.. Evidence: SYN-D.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes carbohydrate accuracy for individuals with diabetes, using the existing direct sales force to reach this segment. Begin with a limited pilot offering a digital kitchen scale with carbohydrate measurement features, and gather willingness-to-pay data before scaling. Target customer: Individual consumers with diabetes who need precise food weight measurements to track carbohydrate intake.. Value proposition: A digital kitchen scale that provides accurate carbohydrate measurements, leveraging Mettler-Toledo’s precision reputation and direct sales channel to capture premium pricing.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Digital Kitchen Scale Preference Test (500 U.S. adults, 10 weeks, €15,000) to measure willingness to pay and purchase intent for a carbohydrate‑accurate versus convenience‑focused scale.. Uncertainty: The size of the market for carbohydrate‑focused digital scales and the willingness of consumers to pay a premium for accuracy remain uncertain. The test will resolve this.. Would change if: If the test shows the convenience scale generates at least 20% higher willingness to pay and purchase intent than the carbohydrate‑accurate scale, we would shift focus to convenience-driven consumer proposition.; If the test yields no significant difference or the carbohydrate scale fails to meet the €5 premium threshold, we would reconsider the investment.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated digital kitchen scale for home food weighing primarily because it provides a more accurate measure of carbohydrate content, which is important for diabetes management. Who benefits: Individual consumers with diabetes who need precise food weight measurements to track carbohydrate intake.. Why behaviour changes: Increased awareness of carbohydrate counting and the need for accurate food weighing drives demand for a digital scale that offers precise measurements.. How value is captured: Mettler-Toledo can capture value by selling a premium-priced digital scale through direct channels, leveraging its brand reputation for precision and its existing sales force.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a digital scale that provides accurate carbohydrate measurements.; Diabetes awareness and carbohydrate counting are growing among home cooks.; Mettler-Toledo can effectively communicate the accuracy advantage to target consumers.. Predictions: In a test offering a digital kitchen scale with carbohydrate measurement features, purchase intent among diabetes patients will be at least 20% higher than for a standard digital scale.; Surveyed consumers will cite carbohydrate accuracy as the primary reason for choosing the product..

T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated digital kitchen scale for home food weighing primarily because it offers convenience and faster weighing compared to manual methods, making it attractive for busy households. Who benefits: Households with limited time for food preparation who need quick, accurate measurements.. Why behaviour changes: Time-saving benefits and the desire for convenience drive demand for a digital scale that reduces weighing time and effort.. How value is captured: Mettler-Toledo can capture value by selling a compact, user-friendly digital scale through direct channels, leveraging its brand for precision and its existing sales force.. Assumptions: Consumers prioritize speed and ease of use over carbohydrate accuracy.; Digital scales are perceived as more convenient than manual scales.; Mettler-Toledo can effectively communicate convenience advantages to target consumers.. Predictions: In a test offering a digital kitchen scale with quick-weighing features, purchase intent among busy households will be at least 20% higher than for a standard digital scale.; Surveyed consumers will cite convenience as the primary reason for choosing the product..

Test "Digital Kitchen Scale Preference Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario and choice-based conjoint analysis.. Sample: 500 U.S. adults recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and self-reported interest in diabetes management and time-constrained households.. Measure: 1) Primary purchase driver: carbohydrate accuracy vs convenience. 2) Willingness to pay premium (price sensitivity). 3) Intent to purchase (binary: would buy).. Predictions: T1: Consumers who cite carbohydrate accuracy as primary driver will show purchase intent at least 20% higher than those who cite convenience.; T2: Consumers who cite convenience as primary driver will show purchase intent at least 20% higher than those who cite carbohydrate accuracy.. Decision rule: If the difference in purchase intent between the two primary driver groups is at least 20 percentage points, proceed to develop a differentiated digital scale targeting that segment. If the difference is less than 20 points, no further investment is justified.. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated digital kitchen scale that emphasizes carbohydrate accuracy for consumers with diabetes, using the existing direct sales force to reach this segment. Conduct a low-cost test (e.g., a choice-based conjoint survey) to validate demand before scaling. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated digital kitchen scale that emphasizes carbohydrate accuracy for consumers with diabetes, using the existing direct sales force to reach this segment. Conduct a low-cost test (e.g., a choice-based conjoint survey) to validate demand before scaling. Target customer: Individual consumers with diabetes who need precise food weight measurements to track carbohydrate intake.. Value proposition: A premium-priced digital scale that provides accurate carbohydrate measurements, leveraging Mettler-Toledo’s brand reputation for precision and existing sales force to deliver the product directly to consumers.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Digital Kitchen Scale Preference Test (500 U.S. adults, 10 weeks, €15,000) to measure purchase intent differences between carbohydrate accuracy and convenience drivers.. Uncertainty: The size of the consumer market for carbohydrate-focused digital scales and the willingness to pay a premium are unknown. The test will resolve whether demand justifies investment.. Would change if: If the test shows purchase intent for convenience-driven buyers at least 20% higher than for carbohydrate accuracy drivers, we would shift focus to convenience and develop a different product.; If the test yields no significant difference or indicates low intent, we would reconsider expansion or alternative routes.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1: Consumers will adopt Ansell gloves for outdoor recreation and gardening if they perceive the gloves as high-performance, durable, and stylish, leading to repeat purchases and premium pricing. Who benefits: Ansell gains higher margins and brand equity by positioning gloves as premium outdoor gear.. Why behaviour changes: Outdoor enthusiasts and gardeners currently use generic gloves; a differentiated design that meets their functional and aesthetic needs will shift purchase from generic to Ansell.. How value is captured: Ansell can charge premium prices and capture value through brand licensing and co‑branding with outdoor brands.. Assumptions: Outdoor recreation and gardening markets are large enough to support a differentiated consumer line.; Consumers are willing to pay a premium for performance and style in protective gloves.; Ansell can design gloves that meet these criteria without compromising protection.. Predictions: Surveyed outdoor enthusiasts will indicate higher intent to purchase Ansell gloves compared to generic gloves.; Sales of a differentiated outdoor‑recreation line will exceed a baseline of 10,000 units per quarter within 12 weeks of launch.; Willingness to pay for a premium price (e.g., 20% above generic gloves) will be higher than for standard industrial gloves..

T2: Healthcare professionals will adopt Ansell gloves for household use if they perceive the gloves as safe, sterile, and comfortable, leading to increased purchase for home and personal tasks. Who benefits: Ansell gains volume sales and brand extension by serving a new consumer segment beyond industrial and healthcare.. Why behaviour changes: Healthcare workers are already used to sterile gloves; if they see a consumer version that meets the same standards, they will transfer the habit of using gloves for work to home activities.. How value is captured: Ansell can sell gloves at a volume price and potentially license the sterile brand to consumer retailers, capturing value through higher unit volume and brand extension.. Assumptions: Healthcare professionals are willing to purchase gloves for non‑work use if they trust the sterility and comfort.; The consumer version will be marketed as a sterile, professional‑grade product rather than a generic household glove.; Distribution channels will be accessible to individual buyers (e.g., online, specialty retailers).. Predictions: Surveyed healthcare professionals will indicate higher intent to purchase Ansell gloves for household use compared to generic gloves.; Sales of a differentiated healthcare‑to‑consumer line will exceed a baseline of 5,000 units per quarter within 12 weeks of launch.; Willingness to pay for a premium price (e.g., 15% above standard gloves) will be higher than for standard industrial gloves..

Test "Consumer Proposition Test: Outdoor vs Healthcare" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with simulated purchase. Sample: 500 respondents: 250 outdoor recreation enthusiasts (aged 25-45, self‑identified as regular hikers, gardeners, cyclists) and 250 healthcare professionals (aged 30-55, self‑identified as nurses, doctors, or medical students) recruited via panel sites.. Measure: 1) Choice of glove type (Ansell branded vs generic) among the two groups. 2) Willingness to pay a premium (percentage points above generic price). 3) Purchase intent (yes/no) for each option.. Predictions: T1: Outdoor group will choose Ansell branded gloves and indicate higher willingness to pay a premium than healthcare group.; T2: Healthcare group will choose Ansell branded gloves and indicate higher willingness to pay a premium than outdoor group.. Decision rule: If outdoor group choice rate ≥ 60% and willingness to pay premium ≥ 15 percentage points → proceed to develop outdoor‑recreation line. If healthcare group choice rate ≥ 60% and willingness to pay premium ≥ 15 percentage points → develop healthcare‑to‑consumer line. If neither group meets both thresholds → no expansion.. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting outdoor recreation and gardening, leveraging Ansell’s existing glove technology and brand reputation. Begin with a limited launch (e.g., 5,000 units per quarter) to test demand and willingness to pay before scaling. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting outdoor recreation and gardening, leveraging Ansell’s existing glove technology and brand reputation. Begin with a limited launch (e.g., 5,000 units per quarter) to test demand and willingness to pay before scaling. Target customer: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts and gardeners (aged 25–45) who currently use generic gloves for protective tasks.. Value proposition: High‑performance, durable gloves designed specifically for outdoor and gardening activities, marketed as a premium, stylish solution that meets functional and aesthetic needs, allowing Ansell to capture higher margins and brand equity.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Consumer Proposition Test (choice‑based conjoint survey) to validate demand and willingness to pay among outdoor enthusiasts before committing to full production.. Uncertainty: The size of the outdoor/gardening market and consumer willingness to pay a premium for branded gloves are unknown. Evidence of strong demand from healthcare professionals for household use is also uncertain.. Would change if: If the test shows <60% of outdoor enthusiasts choose Ansell branded gloves or willingness to pay premium <15 percentage points, we would abandon the outdoor line and focus on healthcare-to‑consumer expansion.; If new evidence shows healthcare professionals are already purchasing gloves for household use at high volumes, we would reconsider the healthcare line.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.
